Hello everybody,

I just struggle a bit (or a bit more) with the more complex models and get confused about what I read and what is shown in the literature.

So my "full" model shape~CS*species*sex is according to the 'anova()'-function the best one explaining most of my variance if compared to "simpler" models.
The output is as following:

                        Df      SS       MS     Rsq       F             Z        Pr(>F)

CS                    1 0.05200 0.052003 0.03257 12.2422  5.1659     1e-04 ***
species             8 0.52131 0.065163 0.32651 15.3404 13.4933     1e-04 ***
sex                   1 0.05200 0.052002 0.03257 12.2419  5.9927      1e-04 ***
CS:species       8 0.06435 0.008043 0.04030  1.8935  3.6992       0.0002 ***
CS:sex             1 0.00540 0.005400 0.00338  1.2712  0.7827       0.2173
species:sex      8 0.05150 0.006438 0.03226  1.5155  2.6089       0.0058 **
CS:species:sex   8 0.04296 0.005370 0.02691  1.2642  1.3734     0.0835 .
Residuals         190 0.80709 0.004248 0.50550

Total                225 1.59661
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

Call: procD.lm(f1 = shape ~ CS * species * sex, iter = 9999, RRPP = T,

    data = gdf_hum, print.progress = F)

So, I have different allometries between species but not sexes, and different sexual dimorphims between the species. And what ever a three-factor interaction could mean...
If I understand it correctly from what I did read also here in this group, I cannot remove any factor from that model as every factor is interacting in some kind with another one, e.g. just have a look on shape~CS+sex to have a look and visualize sex-shape differences.

Dear Antigoni, I found then your paper "Evolutionary History and Not Heterochronic Modifications Associated with Viviparity Drive Head Shape Differentiation in a Reproductive Polymorphic Species, Salamandra salamandra" which deals also with several factors and I think could be compared in methology what I want to do. Actually, I am not able to really figure out the models run for Table 1. It is stated that population is always nested within subspecies. If I ran a nested model e.g. shape~species/sex I get as a result p-values for 'species' and 'species:sex', but not for 'sex' only! But for that kind of model in Table1 'population' is listed separately as variable?! For my understanding in (c) then the interaction term of CS*subsp.*pop. is missing, if I assume a model like shape~CS*subspec./population ?!
Likely I do misunderstand or misinterpret something.

confused regards,
Peter

Peter, I´m not sure how to help here, but for the sake of the general discussion in the list, I need to notify you that the article you mentioned on Salanamders, is absolutely NOT a good example for a general understanding of interaction terms and allometry, as that system is very complex (biologically, that is) and it includes nested factors and not fully overlapping interactive ones. So definitely NOT a good read unless you first understand linear models very well.

I might recommend that you start by reading some more general literature on the subject. Maybe the practical companion to to Geometric Morphometrics for Biologists, written by Mimi Zelditch and Don Swirderski could be a good read for this. You can find it here:

https://www.researchgate.net/publication/328215969_A_Practical_Companion_to_Geometric_Morphometrics_for_Biologists_Running_analyses_in_freely-available_software_Second_Edition

Good luck!

Antigoni

Hello all!

Thank you so much for adding me to the discussion forum!

First off, I want to say that I am just starting in geometric morphometrics in comparison to others here, so please tell me if I am misunderstanding some aspect of GM in my question (or future ones).

I am currently looking to test the integration and modularity of a landmark set including 3 a priori landmark partitions using integration.test and modularity.test. However, I came across some literature that was saying to be wary of using permutation functions without adding a procrustes fit step to each permutation to prevent landmark dependance from developing through the permutation. Do the functions integration.test and modularity.test already account for this? Or is this something that I will have to add to the function myself?

Again, thanks for letting me into the forum and I look forward to discussing more about geomorph!

Kindest regards

Austin

Austin,

I’m not sure what you mean by ‘prevent landmark dependance from developing through the permutation’.  Once the shapes are aligned via GPA, they are in a common coordinate system. That does not change in the permutation step, and as such the functions you mentioned do not include an additional GPA anywhere. The input data should have been aligned via GPA first.

Dean

messages.body_plain:
Austin is talking about, e.g., Klingenberg 2009 (DOI: 10.1111/j.1525-142X.2009.00347.x). The caution mentioned there is that when using a single Procrustes fit for landmark data that consists of two or more modules, the superimposition generates its own covariance across modules (among their respective coordinates). So, for each permuted set of associations between modules, you perform a new superimposition, generating a new set of induced covariances. Not necessary when the blocks are superimposed separately because there is no induced covariance between them.

(Correct me if I'm wrong but...) modularity.test wouldn't superimpose per permutation because the covariance ratio function shuffles assignments of landmarks (or phenotypic values) to blocks, not blocks to specimens. Integration.test... I don't remember. Does the function behave one way if all the phenotype data is in "A" and another if the phenotype data is divided between "A" and "A2"?

Folks,

Just a point of clarification, as this topic comes up rather frequently.

Yes, such a claim was stated in 2009: that separate vs. simultaneous GPA could make a difference. And yes, a single dataset example showed different point-estimates for the RV coefficient, as shown in that paper. But a single empirical example does not analytical theory make.

First, no mathematical proof (i.e., analytically-derived mathematical theory) was proposed to describe what one should do in such cases, and which procedure was preferable to the other. Second, there was no demonstration via simulation to show either the problem or the preferred solution. Thus, the field has languished in this ‘recommendation’ of either/or separate-combined GPA for 10 years without any real theoretical solution. Until proper mathematical or simulation-based evidence is presented, one should follow the simpler course, and perform a single GPA and then perform modularity/integration analyses (that is, if those structures are really sub-structures of a single configuration).

On a related topic there is a new paper just accepted in Evolutionary Biology (Collyer, Davis, Adams) that finally explores the related topic of ‘combining’ landmark datasets across configurations with respect to how one scales them for size. The connection is that here too, a single empirical example ‘proved’ that one approach to scaling might be useful, whereas a full simulation-based investigation showed conclusively that this was not at all the case. Now, whether or not the same may be said of the resulting shape variables for integration and modularity is premature, but I suspect the ‘combine or not combine for GPA’ question will fall in line with the results of the paper above. Time (and importantly simulations) will tell.

Regardless, I urge empiricists not to simply take the word of a publication on how to perform morphometric analyses without the demonstration by simulation or mathematical proof of what that pipeline generates and provides. Math, analytics, and simulations, will ultimately dictate our decisions in this regard.

Dean

Hello Morphometricians,

I was updating the code of a previous project to the new version of geomorph, and am having difficulty in replicating an analysis with the nested.update() function. I have consulted the online vignette (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/geomorph/vignettes/geomorph.assistance.html), which has solved most of my updates except this one. I was hoping someone could indicate me the equivalent code in the new geomorph version for the code I give below. With that it should suffice to tweak out my other functions or create them anew. Hopefully this equivalence also helps out other users.

For context, I have three species divided into three age categories. The code for geomorph v3.0.7 in R v3.5.1 that I want to replicate is the following:

## age and species are factors with three levels
gdfAllo <- geomorph.data.frame(Y.gpa,species=spp,age=age)
allometry <- procD.lm(coords ~log(Csize)*species + species/age,data=gdfAllo,iter=9999)
allometry <- nested.update(allometry, ~species/age)
summary(allometry)
x11();plot(allometry, type = "regression",
           predictor = log(gdfAllo$Csize),
           reg.type = "PredLine",
           pch = 21,
           bg = as.numeric(gdfAllo$species),
           xlab = "lnCS")

Thanks in advance.

Best regards,
Javier

I think you had an older version that had required a bug fix that you did not install and this is the reason for the disparate results.  But as that was 6 versions ago, it is only a guess.

Mike

Dear Alexandre,

I am cc’ing the geomorph google group in this response because it is a question that I think is intriguing for our community.

There are multiple ways to answer this question, but the simplest is no, there is no way to use the step or stepAIC functions on geomorph objects.  Inherent in those functions is the extracAIC function, which can be applied to objects of class lm, glm, aov, etc.  These are all univariate.  Why? I am not sure but suspect its because in order to calculate AIC, one needs to calculate log-likelihoods, and in order to calculate log-likelihoods for multivariate data, one must find the determinant of the residual covariance matrix.  That last part is troublesome if covariance matrices are singular, which is so likely with GM data that we might as well consider it a certainty for a function.  So there is no reliable way to extend geomorph to these other multi-use functions, unless we redefine how to calculate AIC with highly multivariate data, an area of research is strong need of theoretical development.

Alternatively, we could use a different criterion than AIC in a stepwise procedure.  Older methods use P-values and define a criterion, like P < 0.25 to keep terms.  We could possibly create something like this for procD.lm objects, but one would have to define a number of permutations, and every model comparison would require waiting for say, 1000 permutations to run.  Set it up before you go to sleep and get the results in the morning, and try not to be burdened by the inelegance of using P-values (I will not go into the many reasons this is ill-advised here).  This just does not seem worth creating.

So, a stepwise procedure — which I would love to have — is still in the “maybe in the future” stage at this point.

We do have a function in RRPP called model.comparison, that could use separate procD.lm fits (same as lm.rrpp fits) to graphically show the trace of residual covariance matrix or -2 *log-likelihood versus parameter penalty (like is calculated in AIC).  This is descriptive (so is AIC) but is diagnostically helpful.  The only problem is you would have to estimate many models first to compare them (the examples in the help file should be informative for how to set it up).

I might have to think if I can add an algorithm for a stepwise option to this in the future.  I’m not sure it is possible.  But if you are willing to fit several models, you can compare them to find which has the lowest error compared to the expected error based on the number of parameters; i.e., a form of model selection.  I think it is the best option we have for shape data at the moment.

I hope this is helpful, even if the news is disappointing.

Cheers!
Mike

messages.subject: Two methods of shape vector projection, which one to choose
messages.subject_clean: Two methods of shape vector projection, which one to choose
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

Projection of multidimensional shape vector onto another vector is a commonly used technique in GM. Klingenberg used this approach to calculate shape score (The pace of morphological change: historical transformation of skull shape in St Bernard dogs). Likewise, Philipp Gunz used this technique to obtain cranial globularity score that quantifies each specimen's position along the vector representing cranial shape differences between modern and archaic specimens (Neandertal Introgression Sheds Light on Modern Human Endocranial Globularity). Higher globularity score may indicate more modern/archaic cranial shape, depending on the direction of comparison. For both shape score and globularity score, each specimen is given one single value.

In a recent paper by Zaidi et al. (Facial masculinity does not appear to be a conditiondependent male ornament and does not reflect MHC heterozygosity in humans), human facial masculinity is likewise calculated by projecting shape data onto a vector that quantifies differences in consensus facial shape between famales and males (calc_masc_03262018.R file from https://github.com/Arslan-Zaidi/Facial_masculinity_MHC). However, Zaidi performed shape vector projection in a different way.

I illustrate Gunz's and Zaidi's method as below:

In words, Gunz collapsed all coordinates of all landmarks into a single multidimensional vector for projection. In contrast, Zaidi performed the projection landmark-wise to obtained one score for each landmark and averaged the scores across all landmarks to obtain an overall score for each specimen. But the problem is the globscore by Gunz and M_overall score by Zaidi are not numerically identical when the same dataset is analyzed.

Gunz's approach is consistent with how shape score was calculated by tradition. In geomorpho package in R, shape score is calculated through RRPP:::center(as.matrix(Y)) %*% B %*% ((t(B) %*% B) ^ -0.5), where Y contains shape data with n (number of specimens) rows and p*k columns (p landmarks in k dimensions). This is in line with Gunz's approach.

The fascinating aspect of Zaidi's approach is that each landmark is given one score, which facilitates visualization (e.g., Fig 2B allows for color maps to be overlayed onto facial morphs, which allows for statitical assessment and visualization of the effect of covariates on facial masculinity for each landmark. Following Gunz's approach, this is not possible because each specimen is given only one single score).

The question is how should we perceive Zaidi's approach to calculating score for each landmark, is it truely reasonable in GM? In addition, if we do follow Zaidi to estimate shape/globularity/masculinity score for each landmark in our dataset, should we just average scores over landmarks to obtain the overall score or should we still stick to Gunz's approach when calculating overall score?

Kieran

Kieran,

It appears to me that Gunz’s score is calculated following orthogonal projection and Zaidi score is calculated following oblique projection (where axes are allowed to be stretched differently).  The Zaidi score does not appropriately pool the vector lengths like the denominator of the Gunz score does.  The division by 3 seems to attempt to scale the score into a unidimensional score (one could divide the Gunz score by 3, also).  It seems also that because the denominator in each of the three calculations — let’s call these L1, L2, and L3 —  are the three vector lengths, used to make the calculation a score for a projection on a unit length vector, they divided by 3 because they had three vectors.  But to make the projection unit length in all dimensions, the average is not (L1 + L2 + L3)/3; it is sqrt(L1^2 + L2^2 + L3^2)/3, which is the same as the Gunz denominator divided by 3.

So we can disentangle two things.  One difference is the division by 3.  That is arbitrary because if it was only a division by three, the two scores would differ by a scalar constant.  The other thing is how vectors are averaged.  Note that M1 + M2 + M3 produces a numerator that matches the Gunz calculation.  No worry there.  But the Gunz score finds the appropriate vector length in all dimensions; the Zaidi score finds the vector length in each direction and averages them, ignoring Euclidean geometry.  The result is that the axes are allowed to stretch independently to make sure they are all the same length, which turns an orthogonal projection into an oblique one.

I’m not sure I explained this the best way possible, but my inclination would be to trust the Gunz score over the Zaidi score.

Cheers!
Mike

Thank you Kieran for raising this interesting issue and thank you Mike for the explanation. Please allow me to chime in.

Gunz stated in his paper "To quantify globularity, we computed the difference between the Procrustes mean shape of the Neandertal endocrania and the average shape of all modern European endocrania extracted from CT scans. We then projected the Procrustes shape coordinates of all endocrania (i.e., CT and MRI data) onto this multivariate group-difference vector (Figure 2B)." I believe this should be done in exactly the same way in which shape score is estimated in geomorph, i.e., RRPP:::center(as.matrix(Y)) %*% B %*% ((t(B) %*% B) ^ -0.5). Y is a n by p*k matrix (n specimens, p landmarks in k dimensions). For 3D shape data, columns of Y would be x1, y1, z1, x2, y2, z2 ..., xn, yn, zn. The "target specimen" in Kieran's table can be considered as the first row of Y. B would be a matrix of regression coefficients, or equivalently shape difference vector, of p*k rows (coefficients for x1, y1, x2, y2, ..., xn, yn, in this order) and 1 column. In Kieran's case, B would be a1, b1, c1, a2, b2, c2, a3, b3, c3 in 9 rows and 1 column. Therefore, RRPP:::center(as.matrix(Y)) %*% B would mean Gunz performed calculation as x1*a1 + y1*b1 + z1*c1 + x2*a2 + y2*b2 + z2*c2 + x3*a3 + y3*b3 + z3*c3. I do not think it necessary to include all crossproducts. Since Gunz's code is not directly available, I would assume that Gunz did the analysis in the same way shape score was calculated in geomorph. Kirean might have misunderstood Gunz's approach or made a typo by including x1*a2 in his calculation, which should be x2*a2 instead.

What is interesting is Zaidi's approach. I check his source code (attached) and noted that lines 98-112 were most relevant, which I demonstrate here:

It can be seen that qlmasc.mat1 is a matrix of n by 7150 where n is the number of individuals and 7150 is the number of landmarks. Line 104 suggest rows of target.df is projected onto cons.ql, where cons.ql is a row vector of length 3, which corresponds to the 3 coordinates of the landmark (qlindex,qlindex+1,qlindex+2). Line 112 suggests averaging is performed across all landmarks through simple arithmetic mean and this was performed for each row (individual) separately. Kieran correctly illustrated Zaidi's approach of averaging by (M1 + M2 + M3) / 3.

We could probably conclude that Zaidi's approach to perform projections landmark-wise is indeed useful but Gunz's approach is more appropriate when it comes to estimating overall score at individual level. Mike and Kieran, please let me know if I am wrong.

Wen

messages.body_plain:
Using boneLM dataset from Morpho package, I performed GPA using Morpho and geomroph package but found that the results differ.

library(Morpho)
library(geomorph)

require(rgl)
data(boneData)

################################################################################
# Ignoring symmetry
################################################################################
# GPA in Morpho using ProcGPA
procM <- ProcGPA(boneLM, scale = TRUE, reflection = TRUE, CSinit = TRUE,
 pcAlign = TRUE)
dat1 <- procM$rotated

# GPA in geomorph using gpagen
procG <- gpagen(boneLM, ProcD = FALSE, Proj = TRUE)
dat2 <- procG$coords

# Angle calculation
AngleFromMorpho <- c(t(dat1[,,1])) - c(t(dat1[,,3]))
AngleFromGeomorph <- c(t(dat2[,,1])) - c(t(dat2[,,3]))
angle.calc(AngleFromMorpho, AngleFromGeomorph) * (180/pi)
# [1] 126.6105 #The direction representing shape difference between specimen 1 and 3 calculated from both packages differ by 126 degrees. Not in the same direction!

################################################################################
# Considering the symmetric component
################################################################################
# GPA in Morpho using procSym
left <- c(4,6,8)
right <- c(3,5,7)
pairedLM <- cbind(left,right)
symprocM <- procSym(boneLM, scale = TRUE, reflect = TRUE, CSinit = TRUE,
   orp = TRUE, pairedLM = pairedLM, bending = TRUE,
   pcAlign = TRUE)
dat3 <- symprocM$Symtan

# GPA in geomorph using bilat.symmetry
symprocG <- bilat.symmetry(boneLM, land.pairs = pairedLM, object.sym = TRUE,
      ind = 1:dim(boneLM)[3])
dat4 <- symprocG$symm.shape

# Angle calculation
AngleFromMorpho2 <- c(t(dat3[1,])) - c(t(dat3[3,]))
AngleFromGeomorph2 <- c(t(dat4[,,1])) - c(t(dat4[,,3]))
angle.calc(AngleFromMorpho2, AngleFromGeomorph2) * (180/pi)
# [1] 95.43279 #The direction representing symmetric component of shape difference between specimen 1 and 3 calculated from both packages differ by 95 degrees. Not in the same direction!

I have set orthogonal projection in both functions and also using bending energy as the criteria for minimization. However, the direction representing shape difference from the 1st and 3rd specimen calculated from the two packages differ by 126 degrees for total shape and by 95 degrees for the symmetric component. The differences are obviously not trivial. So how should we perceive such difference?

Regards,
Lv

Kieran,

The way you have set up the symmetry analysis does not correspond with your question. It sounds as if you wish to treat each individual at each time point as a separate object. But you have used ind=rep(1,3), … in the formula. That tells the analysis that an individual is replicated 3 times, and of course will find an overall average of them for the symmetric and asymmetric components.

To do what you seem to want, you need to treat each individual at each time point as a separate object. That means using: ind <- seq(1:9), and using no ‘rep’ component.

Obviously, the summary anova table in this case is meaningless, but this will give you the symmetric and asymmetric components of shape for each individual.

messages.body_plain:
Katrien,

It is generally not wise to attempt an interpretation of the % covariation explained by a particular PLS axis: that is forcing PLS into a PCA-way of thinking.

With PCA, there is only one data matrix, and thus there is total variation. Here, one can consider how much is explained on each orthogonal axis and derive some interpretation. However, with PLS, there are two matrices whose covariation is being explained, and a similar logic for interpretation is not straightforward. For instance, one could have very little covariation between the two matrices, but of that little covariation, most is in the first PLS axis. Considering this at a percentage of total covariation then gives the misleading impression that the high percentage is rather impressive. It may not be.

Generally, it is best to stick with the PLS correlation for interpretation. Or better yet, interpret the empirically-derive effect size found from the observed rPLS and its permutation distribution.

Dean

Dear all,

 I am in the early stages of a project that aims to evaluate fluctuating asymmetry (FA) as a measure of developmental instability. To facilitate exploratory tests, I would like to have an individual measure of FA. I am hoping to use the FA.component that is returned from the bilat.symmetry function (obtaining an FA value by calculating the root-sum-of-squares the configurations), but was hoping to understand a little more clearly how FA.component coordinate configurations are calculated.
 Do the FA.component coordinate configurations represent the individual's right-left differences minus the population's average right-left differences? I believe this is a method frequently advocated for isolating fluctuating asymmetry (found in, for example, Zelditch et al. 2012: 369 and Klingenberg and McIntyre 1998: 1375 - the latter being referenced for the bilat.symmetry function). I have looked at the function's code, but have to admit that I am relatively inexperienced in coding and so would appreciate guidance on the subject.
 Best regards,

   Ben W.

messages.body_plain:
Hi all
I have a dataset of 53 cranial landmarks of mammalian crania on which I'm testing 5 different possible modularity schemes.
Using the regular modularity.test indicates that all 5 schemes are significantly different from null (p = 0.001), with CR values between 0.66 and 0.82, and Z values ranging from -3 to -6. Presumably the scheme with the most negative Z score is preferred.

However using the phylo.modularity function indicates that none of these 5 schemes are significant (p ranging from 0.08 to 1), with CR values 0.92 to 1.35, and Z values from -1.5 to +5.5

The differences in result are quite striking, but I'm not sure how to interpret this. It's often the case that comparisons within a phylogenetic context are to be preferred, but I can't find examples of others using this specific phylogenetic modularity test.

I also tried running modularity.test on the phylogenetically independent contrasts of my procrustes-transformed landmark dataset. The results are closer to the non-phylogenetic modularity test (and this makes sense to me).

Any thoughts on why the phylo.modularity function produces such different results than a PIC approach?

Thanks

Faysal

If I can rephrase your question, you are asking why you have one result when ignoring phylogenetic nonindependence and get a different result when phylogeny is taken into account.  This can happen, and is particularly acute in datasets where interspecific trends also covary with phylogenetic relatedness. When this happens, phylogeny has confounded the signal, and an analysis ignoring phylogeny is incorrect.

I suggest a careful reading of the basic statistical literature on phylogenetic comparative methods, starting with Felsenstein 1985 (Am Nat). Recent reviews of PCMs for morphometric data (e.g., Adams and Collyer 2019: Ann. Rev.; 2018: Syst. Biol.) have additional references.

I have an update on this if anyone else runs into this issue. I tested whether things were going wrong because I was using na.omit within the function by using it instead to create a new list of dataframes (one for each lake) without missing values or unused variables. Then I ran that through the function.

here is that new code:
lapply(split.adj.data,function(x){
  modularity.test(x,c('a','a','a','a','a','a','a','b','b','b','c','c','c','c','c','d','d','d'),CI=T)
})
It turns out that na.omit wasn't the issue, and the presence of missing values wasn't either.

What did cause problems were two vectors of data describing meristic traits within one of the partition groups (which included a total of 7 variables). Within some lakes, neither of those two meristic traits varied at all, and in those lakes, removing one or both of those variables produced normal modularity.test results.

I am still not sure of the specific problem given that leaving in one but not both of these non-varying traits produces normal results, but this is a step in the right direction, I guess.

Grant

messages.subject_clean: On incommensurate units and scale: CR and other analyses
messages.body_plain:
Grant et al.,

Grant’s original question concerned application of a particular method (the CR) for his data, which contained both continuous and meristic count data. However, the real issue is not a ‘failing’ of a particular method to handle someone’s data, but rather rests in the logic of asking mathematics to do something it cannot. This issue pertains much more broadly to quantitative analysis in general, and since we receive queries that boil down to this issue several times a year, it is time to revisit this discussion again.

With all multivariate analyses, one must have data of commensurate types, of commensurate units, and in commensurate scale. Otherwise, the analysis is simply GIGO.  The reason is that multivariate analyses ultimately ask about the locations of objects in a multivariate dataspace: their similarity and difference, the trait correlation and covariation, etc.  That requires a distance measure (recall that covariances and distances are intimately related mathematically: see Gower 1966: so even if the analysis is about trait correlations/covariances, mathematically this is asking about distances [albeit of variables]). So only data of commensurate types can be combined for a multivariate analysis.

As an example, say one has a binary trait (0/1), meristic counts (1,2,3), and a continuous variable. Technically all of these variables contain numbers, so surely one can perform a principal components analysis on them right?  WRONG! (well, one could, but one should not).  Binary traits are in a dataspace defined by Hamming distance (or another binary distance measure), counts are in a space of Gower distances, and continuous data may be in a space defined by Euclidean distance.  It makes no biological or mathematical sense to combine these and try to understand similarity of differences among objects; the math simply does not work.

Importantly, this issue can even occur when one has all continuous variables. Say we have temperature, elevation, and relative humidity. Surely we can obtain an ordination to show similarities amongst localities?  Well…. Maybe, but not in their original units. Temperature (C), elevation (m), relative humidity (g/m^3) are in incommensurate units and scale. So what does a covariance mean in this context? How does one interpret (deviations in C * deviations in g/m^3)? One cannot. Same thing with a distance, which is also based on those deviations. And for some of these variables (temperature), once could use other units that convey the same relative information but stretch that axis; which in turn stretches a sub-dimension of the dataspace. Not good. Now commensurate units could be obtained from continuous variables if they are converted to their standard normal deviates; and in this case they could be combined. However, in their original units/scale they should not (and standard normal deviates will not resolve the issue of different data types: binary, meristic, continuous).

If one ponders their particular discipline (ecology, evolutionary biology, psychometrics, anthropology, etc.), I’m sure one can come up with many published examples of the above infractions. Put simply, errors of this type abound in many quantitative disciplines. But being aware of this is important so as not to repeat these same errors. Such spaces simply cannot be interpreted mathematically or biologically, meaning the resulting ordination, MANOVA, CR, etc. cannot be interpreted. For a discussion of these in the context of dataspaces and ordination see: Legendre and Legendre, 2012 (ecology side) and Adams and Collyer, 2019 (evolution side).

Folks, one must understand that this is not a failing of a method or even of mathematics. It is simply asking math to do something it cannot. One cannot interpret combined datasets when those variables are of incommensurate type, units, or scale. Complicated workarounds could be envisioned, but are well beyond the general scope of discussion; and these have not been fully vetted  mathematically to demonstrate that they do what is intended.

The short answer is: just don’t do it.

Best,

Dean

Thanks for the response, but I’m aware of PCMs, and my question was more specifically about the phylo.modularity function.

Let me try this a different way: why might the results using phylo.modularity differ significantly from an approach using PIC?

Below is an example using the attached testdata.Rdata file. Results for non-phylogenetic and PIC of landmark data are similar (modularity present, p=0.001) while the phylo.modularity test indicates it is not (p=1, CR>1).

Adams & Felice 2014 discusses some differences between PIC vs PGLS evolutionary covariance matrix approaches, but can this produce such different results on the same dataset?
Perhaps I’m missing something obvious here…?

Thanks again.

##
library(geomorph)
library(ape)

coords.test <- test.data$coords.test #53 3D landmarks, 10 species
partitions <- test.data$partitions #partition scheme with 6 modules
tree <- test.data$tree

# Non-phylogenetic modularity test
non.ph.mod <- modularity.test(coords.test, partition.gp <http://partition.gp>=partitions)

# Phylogenetic modularity test
ph.mod <- phylo.modularity(coords.test, partition.gp <http://partition.gp>=partitions, phy=tree, CI = FALSE, iter=499)

# PIC modularity test
coords.2d <- two.d.array(coords.test)
pic.mat <- apply(coords.2d, 2, pic, phy=tree) #PIC landmark matrix
pic.mat <- arrayspecs(pic.mat, 53,3)
pic.mod <- modularity.test(pic.mat, partition.gp <http://partition.gp>=partitions)

# Compare results
cbind(non.ph.mod, pic.mod, ph.mod)

See Adams and Collyer 2015 Evolution (the ‘what you shuffles matters’ paper). Shuffling PICs is not correct for linear models, and is correct here. Thanks for the response, but I’m aware of PCMs, and my question was more specifically about the phylo.modularity function.

Let me try this a different way: why might the results using phylo.modularity differ significantly from an approach using PIC?

Below is an example using the attached testdata.Rdata file. Results for non-phylogenetic and PIC of landmark data are similar (modularity present, p=0.001) while the phylo.modularity test indicates it is not (p=1, CR>1).

Adams & Felice 2014 discusses some differences between PIC vs PGLS evolutionary covariance matrix approaches, but can this produce such different results on the same dataset?

Perhaps I’m missing something obvious here…?

Thanks again.

##

library(geomorph)

library(ape)

coords.test <- test.data$coords.test #53 3D landmarks, 10 species

partitions <- test.data$partitions #partition scheme with 6 modules

tree <- test.data$tree

# Non-phylogenetic modularity test

non.ph.mod <- modularity.test(coords.test, partition.gp <http://partition.gp>=partitions)

# Phylogenetic modularity test

ph.mod <- phylo.modularity(coords.test, partition.gp <http://partition.gp>=partitions, phy=tree, CI = FALSE, iter=499)

# PIC modularity test

coords.2d <- two.d.array(coords.test)

pic.mat <- apply(coords.2d, 2, pic, phy=tree) #PIC landmark matrix

pic.mat <- arrayspecs(pic.mat, 53,3)

pic.mod <- modularity.test(pic.mat, partition.gp <http://partition.gp>=partitions)

# Compare results

cbind(non.ph.mod, pic.mod, ph.mod)

##

messages.body_plain:
If one has interspecific data, then non-phylogenetic analyses of modularity or integration are not recommended.

As for PICs, they may be used in comparative analyses. However, be aware that any approaches using permutations must be done on the correct exchangeable units. Using permutations of PICs can get one into trouble, as shown in that 2015 paper.

The alternative is phylogenetic transformation + RRPP, which is what our procedures utilize. Phylogenetic transformation yields identical parameter estimates to those found from PICs or PGLS, but has the advantage of having residuals that are the correct exchangeable units under the null hypothesis for the test (see Adams and Collyer, 2018: Evolution on phylogenetic ANOVA).

> On 27. May 2020, at 21:37, Adams, Dean [EEOB] <dca...@iastate.edu> wrote:
>

> If one has interspecific data, then non-phylogenetic analyses of modularity or integration are not recommended.
>
> As for PICs, they may be used in comparative analyses. However, be aware that any approaches using permutations must be done on the correct exchangeable units. Using permutations of PICs can get one into trouble, as shown in that 2015 paper.
>
> The alternative is phylogenetic transformation + RRPP, which is what our procedures utilize. Phylogenetic transformation yields identical parameter estimates to those found from PICs or PGLS, but has the advantage of having residuals that are the correct exchangeable units under the null hypothesis for the test (see Adams and Collyer, 2018: Evolution on phylogenetic ANOVA).
>
